title: A Scale to Measure Social and Economic Conservatism
text:
Researchers across several fields make extensive use of the concept of ideology. Yet despite its ubiquity, ideology continues to be measured with scales that carry substantial conceptual and methodological problems. I propose a new scale for identifying social and economic conservatism that treats the two as distinct dimensions rather than points on a single continuum. The scale measures conservatism directly rather than through evaluative proxies, requires no specialized political knowledge of respondents, and is shorter than traditional instruments while retaining enough items to avoid truncation. Because it draws on ANES items rather than ad hoc measures such as feeling thermometers, it also supports comparison across decades. Replicating past research on affective polarization, I show the scale generates important complementary insights for researchers studying ideology.

Thesis. Master of Arts Program in the Social Sciences, University of Chicago.
Presented. American Politics Workshop, University of Chicago — Fall 2019.

title: Preferment Without Partisanship: Ideology and Connectivity in the U.S. Catholic Episcopal Network
text:
Social Network Analysis has been proposed as a way into the cultures of preferment, patronage, and reciprocal obligation that shape the Catholic episcopate. Bullivant and Sadewo’s exploratory study of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales and the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called for extensions linking network position to other attributes of bishops. This project takes up that invitation. I attach ideal point estimates for U.S. Catholic bishops to their directed co-citation network, restricting the analysis to the subgraph of bishops for whom scores are available. Connectivity does not track ideology. The rank correlation between total degree and ideology is weak and does not survive scrutiny: the Pearson correlation points the other way, degree takes few distinct values across the matched network, and mean ideology is flat across degree bands. Splitting by direction locates what little signal there is in outdegree rather than indegree, on the coarser of the two measures. Whatever organizes this network — geography, seniority, committee service — it does not appear to be left-right ideology, and there is no evidence of ideologically sorted cliques.

Status. Work in progress, actively under development.
Data. Network data from Bullivant and Sadewo, “Power, Preferment, and Patronage: An Exploratory Study of Catholic Bishops and Social Networks.” Ideal point estimates from Ideology and Priorities in an Organizational Hierarchy.

title: Rubén Rodríguez Barrón
text:
I am a PhD candidate in the Department of Political Science at the University of Chicago, focusing on American politics. My research lies at the intersection of religion and public opinion, with particular attention to the political behavior of American Catholics. My dissertation examines how Catholics’ political preferences have evolved since the Second Vatican Council and the extent to which they align with the agenda of the USCCB. Using a combination of historical analysis, diocesan-level studies, and survey data, I investigate how elite-mass linkages within the Church shape political outcomes.
My broader research interests include the evolution of ideology and partisanship in the United States, elite-mass communication, political media, the politicization of entertainment, and the effects of polarization on governance. I have a strong methodological foundation, holding a Certificate in Computational Social Science and extensive training in statistical modeling, R and Python programming, and data visualization.
Prior to entering academia, I worked in the finance industry in both executive and advisory roles, including at CEMEX and Ernst & Young. I also co-founded a consulting firm delivering CFO services to small and family-owned businesses. My teaching experience spans over a decade, ranging from university-level instruction in accounting, finance, and business ethics in Mexico to undergraduate and graduate lecturing at the University of Chicago. As a preceptor, I have advised theses in the MA Program in the Social Sciences (MAPSS), the Harris School of Public Policy, and the Department of Political Science. I have also served repeatedly as a teaching and research assistant across a variety of disciplines.
I hold a Master of Arts in Social Sciences and a master’s in political science from the University of Chicago, a master’s in professional accounting from the University of Texas at Austin, and dual bachelor’s degrees in accounting and finance from the Instituto Tecnológico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey (ITESM), where I graduated with honors.
I live in Hyde Park with my wife and two children.

title: Ideology and Priorities in an Organizational Hierarchy: Evidence from US Catholic Bishops
text:
Scholarship on elite ideology has relied on roll-call votes, campaign contributions, and self-placement. Little is known about elites who leave none of these. I present the first ideological measure of U.S. Catholic bishops, estimated with a Bayesian Bradley-Terry model from 1,283 pairwise comparisons elicited from seminarians, clergy, and other informed Catholic elites. The scores place 277 bishops on the same five-point scale priests use for themselves in the National Study of Catholic Priests. The American Catholic hierarchy is concentrated, not polarized. Its perceived spread is a fifth of the priests’. Twenty-seven bishops in the tails carry four fifths of the variance. Appointing pope, Roman education, rite, rank, religious order, and the party of the U.S. president at appointment all fail to sort bishops. No bishop score correlates above 0.11 with forty-five measures of priests’ priorities, ministries, and conduct. An elite this unpolarized is one whose cues theory expects to be weak.

Presented.

“Ideological Variation Among U.S. Catholic Bishops: Scores, Networks, and Electoral Implications” — Midwestern Political Science Association, Chicago, IL, Spring 2026
“The Political Ideology of Catholic Bishops” — Research and Analysis in the Sociology of Religion, University of Notre Dame, Fall 2025

title: The Decline of Catholic Electoral Distinctiveness in U.S. Presidential Elections, 1948–2024
text:
Catholics were once among the most reliably Democratic constituencies in American politics. Using the American National Election Studies Cumulative File, I track Catholic presidential vote choice across twenty elections from 1948 to 2024. The Catholic Democratic advantage peaked in 1960, narrowed steadily, and reversed: by 2024 Catholics were slightly less Democratic than the electorate as a whole. Blinder-Oaxaca decompositions and nested logistic models show that party identification is the primary mediator of this decline, with ideology and issue attitudes absorbing much of what remains. Affect toward social groups mediates further, and the residual Catholic coefficient turns negative once it is controlled. The aggregate trend conceals a divided electorate: white Catholics have moved Republican while Hispanic Catholics have not, observant Catholics have moved right while nominal Catholics have not, and generational replacement compounds both. Catholics remain cross-pressured, culturally conservative and economically progressive in a way that maps cleanly onto neither party. A multilevel model with partial pooling finds no stable, time-invariant Catholic effect on Democratic voting. Catholic electoral exceptionalism is a historically bounded phenomenon rather than a permanent feature of American politics.

Presented.

“The Politics of American Catholics” — New Directions in American History, University of Chicago, Spring 2026
